questions.question: What must happen to every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ if $\mathbb{F}$ is algebraically closed?
options: It must factor into linear factors over a larger field only
It must have no roots in $\mathbb{F}$
It must have at least one root in $\mathbb{F}$
It must have only integer coefficients

questions.question: Why does the definition specify “nonconstant polynomial”?
options: Because constant polynomials always have infinitely many roots in $\mathbb{F}$
Because a linear polynomial over $\mathbb{F}$ may have no root in $\mathbb{F}$
Because constant polynomials are not elements of $\mathbb{F}[x]$
Because nonzero constant polynomials never have a root in $\mathbb{F}$

questions.question: Which field is algebraically closed?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$
$\mathbb{Z}$
$\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{C}$

questions.question: Which field is not algebraically closed?
options: $\mathbb{C}$
An algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$
$\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Where must the root of a polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ lie?
options: Only inside $\mathbb{R}$
Outside the coefficient field
Inside the same field $\mathbb{F}$
Only inside $\mathbb{N}$

questions.question: Why does $x^2+1$ show that $\mathbb{R}$ is not algebraically closed?
options: It is constant
It is not a polynomial
It has no complex root
It has no real root

questions.question: What are the roots of $x^2+1$ in $\mathbb{C}$?
options: $\mathrm{i}$ and $-\mathrm{i}$

questions.question: If $\mathbb{F}$ is algebraically closed and $p(x)\in\mathbb{F}[x]$ has degree $3$, what is guaranteed?
options: $p$ is the zero polynomial
$p$ has a root in $\mathbb{F}$
$p$ has no roots in $\mathbb{F}$
$p$ has exactly three distinct roots in $\mathbb{F}$

questions.question: Which polynomial is the usual example for testing whether $\mathbb{R}$ is algebraically closed?
Over $\mathbb{Q}$, the polynomial $x^2-2$ has no rational root. What does this show about $\mathbb{Q}$?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$ is algebraically closed
Every polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ is constant
$\mathbb{Q}$ is not algebraically closed
$x^2-2$ is not in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$

questions.question: What is the intuitive meaning of saying that a field is algebraically closed?
options: It solves all polynomial equations over that field.
It is closed under addition, multiplication and division.
Each polynomial equation over it has exactly one solution.
Only its quadratic equations are guaranteed to be solvable.

questions.question: What stronger factorization property follows by repeatedly applying the root condition in an algebraically closed field?
options: Every nonconstant polynomial is irreducible over the field.
Every nonconstant polynomial splits into linear factors.
Every nonconstant polynomial is a power of one linear factor.
Every polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ distinct roots in it.

questions.question: Why is algebraic closedness a property of the chosen field, not just of the displayed formula?
options: A polynomial may have a root in a larger field, not the original.
Whether a root exists depends only on the degree.
A polynomial has the same roots in every field containing it.
Closedness depends only on whether the coefficients are integers.

questions.question: Let $p(x)=x^4+2x+7\in\mathbb{C}[x]$. What is guaranteed by algebraic closedness of $\mathbb{C}$?
options: $p$ has at least one real root
$p$ has exactly four real roots
$p$ has at least one rational root
$p$ has at least one complex root

questions.question: In an algebraically closed field $\mathbb{F}$, how can a quadratic $x^2+bx+c$ be factored in $\mathbb{F}[x]$?
options: Only if $b=c=0$
Only as a quadratic with no root in $\mathbb{F}$
As a product of linear factors over $\mathbb{F}$
Never as a product involving roots

questions.question: A field $\mathbb{F}$ has a degree-$5$ polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ with no root in $\mathbb{F}$. What follows?
options: $\mathbb{F}$ is algebraically closed
$\mathbb{F}$ is not algebraically closed
$\mathbb{F}$ must be finite
The degree must actually be zero

questions.question: Why does the definition not say that every polynomial must have all its roots distinct?
options: Repeated roots are not roots
It requires roots to exist, allowing repeats.
Polynomials over fields cannot have repeated roots.
Distinct roots are required only over $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: If a field is algebraically closed, why is there no need to enlarge the field to find a root of a nonconstant polynomial over it?
options: The definition already guarantees a root inside the field
Every nonconstant polynomial over the field is already linear
Its roots are always real, so no complex numbers are needed
A field that is algebraically closed has no larger fields

questions.question: Which observation is enough to prove that a field $\mathbb{F}$ is not algebraically closed?
options: A nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ has no root in $\mathbb{F}$.
A nonzero constant polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ has no root in $\mathbb{F}$.
A nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ has no root in $\mathbb{R}$.
A polynomial in $\mathbb{F}[x]$ has fewer distinct roots than its degree.

questions.question: Let $\mathbb{F}$ be algebraically closed and let $p(x)\in\mathbb{F}[x]$ have degree $n\ge 1$. What factorization form is consistent with the definition?
options: $p(x)=c(x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_n)$ with $a_i,c\in\mathbb{F}$ and $c\ne0$
$p(x)$ has no roots unless $n=1$
$p(x)$ cannot be factored into linear terms when $n>1$
$p(x)$ must have coefficients outside $\mathbb{F}$
